summary: A strong discovery call with textbook current-state, future-state, and compelling-event work — Jordan built a clear, buyer-owned picture of the data-trust problem and its board-level stakes. The deal is being left on the table at the finish: impact never became a defensible ROI number, the decision process is only half-mapped, and the call closed without a calendared next step or committed stakeholders. Biggest lever: convert the impact into a dollar model and lock a specific next meeting with Finance and Operations.

strengths.title: Layered discovery that earned the truth
strengths.detail: Jordan didn't accept the first answer. He moved from a surface complaint ('not really') down through specific examples, duration, and prior attempts to fix — the buyer ended up articulating the pain, the trust spiral, and the cost themselves. That's the discovery doing the selling.

strengths.title: Future-state framing that made the gap vivid

improvements.title: Close on a calendared next step, not a summary
improvements.detail: After excellent discovery, the call ended with 'send me a summary' — an open loop with no date and no commitment. A document is not a next step; a meeting on the calendar is. This is the single biggest risk to the deal.

improvements.title: Turn the impact into a number a CFO would accept
improvements.detail: Jordan got hours (15/week) and a gut figure ('hundreds of thousands') but didn't co-build a defensible model. Before the Series B board, Sam will need a number he can defend. Anchor it together on the call so it's the buyer's number, not the vendor's.

improvements.better_move: Let's make that concrete. Fifteen hours a week is ~0.4 of an analyst — call it $X of loaded cost a year just in wrangling. Add the two or three resource decisions you'd have made differently — what would one of those have been worth? If we land around $Y, is that the number you'd be comfortable taking to the board?

improvements.title: Secure the stakeholders, don't outsource the multi-thread
improvements.detail: Jordan correctly identified that Finance and Operations own sign-off, then left it to Sam to 'feel it out.' Single-threaded deals stall. Make it easy and low-risk for Sam to bring them in now, while the pain is hot.

Then if it resonates, the three of you join the Friday session. What's the best way to get on her radar?

improvements.title: Map the decision process, not just the people
improvements.detail: Knowing who signs off is half of it. The steps, criteria, and budget remain unknown — the budget question got deflected and wasn't revisited from a different angle. You don't need an exact number, but you do need the shape of how a yes happens.

improvements.better_move: No problem on exact budget. Help me understand the path instead: if you and the team decided this was worth doing, what would the steps to a signed agreement look like — and is there budget allocated for this kind of project this year, or would it need to be carved out?

next_call_focus: Get a specific 30-minute meeting on the calendar before this call ends — don't let 'send a summary' be the next step.
Co-build a one-line ROI number Sam can defend to his board (loaded analyst cost + cost of bad decisions).
Get the VP of Finance and Head of Operations into the next session, framed around the Series B board-prep angle.

manager_notes: High-quality discovery rep; the gap is consistently at the close, not the open. Coaching to 'always leave with a calendared multi-stakeholder next step' would likely move several deals. Strong, dated compelling event here (Series B, end of Q3) — worth inspecting in the forecast.
